claims.text: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a strong caloric response under applied magnetic fields.
(MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits a strong caloric response under applied pressure fields.
The unchanged alloy has poor load-bearing integrity, low ductility, and a tendency to crack.
A post-solidification annealing treatment can induce fine, coherent nanoprecipitates uniformly dispersed in the alloy matrix.
A thermomechanical treatment can form an evenly dispersed secondary phase in a high-entropy-alloy matrix.
claims.field: supporting evidence rationale implicit in intervention

claims.text: Uniformly dispersed coherent nanoprecipitates impede dislocation motion.
Uniformly dispersed coherent nanoprecipitates impede crack propagation.
Formation of a dispersed secondary phase can increase hardness or mechanical strength in a high-entropy alloy.
The proposed nanoprecipitates provide precipitation strengthening that increases yield strength.
The nanoprecipitate-forming anneal also produces grain refinement.
Precipitation strengthening and grain refinement increase fracture toughness.
Maintaining precipitate coherency and avoiding disturbance of the caloric phase transformation preserves caloric performance.
Relative to the as-cast alloy, annealing will increase load-bearing strength by 20–50%.
Relative to the as-cast alloy, annealing will increase fracture toughness by 20–50%.
After annealing, adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change will remain within ±10% of the as-cast value.
The intervention is applicable when magnetic or pressure fields and operating temperature coincide with the reversible caloric transformation.
The treatment is only suitable if it does not perturb the phase equilibrium responsible for the caloric response.
The annealing temperature, duration, and cooling rate required to obtain the desired nanoprecipitate distribution are undetermined.
Long-term operational cycling may alter the microstructure and affect mechanical or caloric performance.

contradictions.description: The predicted mechanical improvement is 20–50%, but the hypothesis is falsified only when improvement is not greater than 15%. An improvement between 15% and 20% would miss the stated prediction while not satisfying the falsification rule.
